DDD Colour Deck

Colour Grading Deck

Dinner,
Diamonds
& Death

Directed & Script Edited by Will Jarvis

Written by Sean Nwachukwu & Adam Sorrell

Draft 16 · ~18 minutes · 35 scenes

Overall Direction

Every location in the film has its own colour world. The audience should feel the temperature change each time we cut somewhere new. The grade is grounded and naturalistic in the wides, then gets more expressionistic in the close-ups as things escalate. Red starts as a background accent and ends up flooding the entire frame by the final shot. Each location wants its own identity, so you can tell where you are from the palette before anyone speaks.

01

Gary's Flat

Olive-amber, sickly, not cosy

Grading Direction

The footage already has a murky olive-brown undertone, which is great. Lean into it. This flat needs to feel unhealthy. Like a low-grade fever, not a fireplace. There's nothing warm or inviting about this place.

  • Shadows pushed toward muddy olive-green
  • Highlights slightly amber but muted, desaturated
  • Skin tones subtly off, not horror-green, just a bit unwell
  • The red chair in Shot 18 is the only vivid element in the space
Push Toward
Reference — Barton Fink (1991)

The Hotel Earle. Wallpaper sweating, everything the colour of old amber and old sweat. Claustrophobia expressed through palette.

Reference — Trainspotting (1996)

The grimy interiors. Sickly greens and yellows making everyday spaces feel unpleasant and run-down. That cheap, slightly nauseating domestic atmosphere.

02

Angelo's Restaurant

Two levels, two colour worlds

Upstairs: Warm Amber-Gold

The restaurant's legitimate face. Clean amber-gold, refined, relatively bright. Angelo's white shirt is the brightest element in the room, which feels right for a man trying to stay clean in a dirty business.

  • Clean amber-gold throughout, not greenish
  • Angelo's white shirt glows
  • Graffiti murals slightly desaturated so they sit in the background

Downstairs: Green Neon

The descent into the basement is immediately felt in the grade. The "BASEMENT LIQUOR" neon is the dominant light source, and it washes everything. The idea is that everything above ground looks better than what's below.

  • Green neon as the dominant colour cast
  • Angelo's white shirt glows almost radioactive against the green
  • Deeper shadows than upstairs, pools of black between the green
Upstairs
Downstairs
Reference — Moonlight (2016)

The diner scene. Warm amber-gold, intimate. The light on skin feels like the room is holding them. This is the warmth we're going for upstairs.

Reference — Chungking Express (1994)

Green fluorescent light contaminating a cramped, tiled kitchen. Intimate, lived-in, slightly grubby. The green spills across everything, including the skin tones.

Reference — Oldboy (2003)

Industrial corridors, dirty green tones, worn surfaces and pockets of near-black. Harsher and more oppressive, but the treatment of the shadows and practical lights is useful for the basement.

03

Hans's Basement

Grey to amber to deep crimson

Grading Direction

This is the most important colour arc in the film. The basement starts harsh, flat, and grey, then progressively fills with red until the final scene is drenched in crimson. The red isn't motivated by a light source. It comes from the grade itself, representing the violence seeping into the frame.

Early (Shots 10, 11, 13, 15)

  • Desaturated and ugly. Grey concrete, harsh bare-bulb light
  • Skin tones washed out, unflattering. Hard deep shadows

Mid: The Chess Game (Shot 24)

  • Amber warmth enters, then tips into red
  • Shadows shift from grey to deep crimson

Late: Reunion & Checkmate (Shots 27, 28, 30)

  • Full red wash, the entire frame tinted crimson
  • Shot 30 is the maximum. Alexis at camera, shotgun raised. The last colour you see
Early
Mid
Late
Reference — Only God Forgives (2013)

The corridor. Amber-red, oppressive, a single colour colonising the frame. This is the transition, the warmth before the red takes over completely.

Reference — The Batman (2022)

The Iceberg Lounge. Deep red, haze, bodies in silhouette. This is the destination, where the basement ends up by checkmate.

Red Progression

The red builds gradually. The audience should only realise the frame has filled with crimson when it's already overwhelming. It starts as an accent and ends as a flood.

04

The Apartment

Cold blue-grey, clinical, a glass cage

Grading Direction

Cold, clinical, sterile. White walls, minimal furniture, floor-to-ceiling windows. The Docklands skyline through the glass provides warm amber dots, but they're distant and unreachable. Violence looks wrong in this space, which is the point.

  • Strong blue-grey push throughout
  • White walls read cold, not warm. No yellow creep
  • City lights through windows: amber-gold but distant, not colouring the interior
  • Skin tones cooler than natural. The apartment drains warmth
  • Blood in Shot 21 is vivid red against the cold grey floor. Keep it vivid

The Balcony (Shots 22, 23)

Part of the apartment world. The grade is consistent between both angles. Night, high-rise, the Docklands skyline behind.

Night
Day (Shot 25)
Reference — Skyfall (2012)

The Shanghai skyscraper fight. Silhouettes against neon through floor-to-ceiling glass. Cold blue, the city as abstract backdrop. Beautiful and lifeless.

05

London Streets

Desaturated, sodium, naturalistic

Grading Direction

The ordinary world. Suburban streets at night with sodium streetlights burning hot orange against crushed darkness. Flat, documentary, unforgiving. Characters feel small against the dark.

  • Crush the shadows. Pools of black between streetlights
  • Sodium orange burns hot but the rest stays cold and dark
  • Desaturated overall. Mute the greens of hedges and gardens
  • Almost CCTV quality: flat, surveillance-like
Push Toward
Reference — Nightcrawler (2014)

Night driving through Los Angeles. Cold, clean, sodium streetlights on a windscreen. The city as a predator's hunting ground.

06

Davina's House

Near-monochrome, domestic, uneasy

Grading Direction

Davina's house is her domestic world, and it feels emptied of life. Nearly monochrome. The key image is the bathroom with its black-and-white chequered tile floor, which echoes the chess motif from the basement. The chess game escapes Hans's world and infects Davina's.

  • Drain nearly all colour. Push toward monochrome
  • Cool daylight through frosted glass, flat and unforgiving
  • Black-and-white tiles dominate the frame graphically
  • Just enough colour left that you sense warmth in the skin but can't quite see it. The ghost of colour, not the absence
Push Toward
Reference — Hereditary (2018)

The house interiors. Uneasy, muted, domestic spaces that feel wrong without anything obviously wrong in the frame. Ordinary rooms with the warmth pulled out.

Shot 29 00:17:06
NOTE The desaturation here is deliberate and thematic, not a technical error. The chess motif in the tiles connects this domestic space back to the basement.
